newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Boeing confident EU will OK deal.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Boeing confident EU will OK deal.

text.p: A Boeing Co. executive said on Thursday he remains confident the European Commission will approve the company's planned acquisition of McDonnell Douglas Corp despite the commission's stated objections.

Raymond Waldmann, Boeing vice president for international business, said he did not know how the aerospace giant would proceed if the U.S. Federal Trade Commission approves the deal but the governing body of the European Union rejects it or withholds approval.
"We hope we don't get to that," Waldmann said. "We do think both sides will approve the merger -- that is still the most likely outcome."

Late Wednesday Boeing received a formal document from the EU outlining objections to the merger, most of which had been well publicized previously in speeches and public statements by European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert.
Waldmann questioned whether the EU has jurisdiction to block the deal, which he characterized as primarily a combination of two U.S. defense contractors.
"That's essentially how we view this," he said. "That's the rationale for this -- to combine our future programs on the defense side with McDonnell Douglas' current programs."

A Boeing position paper, prepared before the the EU's 44-page "statement of objections" was delivered, declares that any effort by the European Commission to block the planned $14 billion merger would raise "serious" issues of jurisdiction.

"EC enforcement action against the merger in this case would contradict both the spirit and the letter" of a 1991 agreement between the European Union and the United States on application of competition laws, Boeing said in the 13-page position paper, made available on Thursday.
"The merger is so clearly a United States transaction that it would be contrary to reasonable expectations for the EC to take enforcement action," Boeing said.

Boeing said in its position paper that based on the 1991 agreement, "it is clear that the merger involves important interests of the United States that would be jeopardized if the EC were to take action."
"Waldmann did not rule out the possibility of negotiating with the EU.

"We know the commission has operated in that mode before," he said. When Boeing Chairman and Chief Executive Phil Condit met with Van Miert in March, the European official repeatedly said "it is up to the company to suggest remedies for issues," Waldmann said.
He said Boeing had not yet decided on a whether to offer any such remedies but would file a written response to the EU objections in about two weeks.
"This is just part of their process." Waldmann said. "It's like an indictment in a criminal trial, but it's not a decision."
A formal hearing is scheduled to be held in Brussels June 12 and June 13 and the commission is expected to make its final decision in late June or early July, Waldmann said.
